Formal conditions: connected, acyclic, single-headed, (usually) projective

intro.why: Dependency trees directly encode who did what to whom, which is what information extraction, question answering and relation extraction need. The two parsing paradigms here (fast greedy transitions vs global graph search) are a recurring trade-off in structured prediction.

sections.title: Why dependencies: free word order
sections.plain: Describe sentences by word-to-word relations instead of nested phrase boxes.
sections.body:
Constituency trees describe nested phrases; for "I saw the man on the hill in Texas with the telescope at noon on Monday" a CFG yields 132 trees, each a deep bracket structure. And in free-word-order languages (Hindi, Russian, Czech, Latin) the same relations appear in many orders, so phrase-structure rules multiply. Hindi "Ram-ne Sita-ko kitaab di" (Ram gave Sita a book) can be reordered because case markers (ne, ko) carry the roles.

Dependency grammar instead links words by binary, asymmetric relations. Picture a solar system: the main verb is the sun; subjects and objects are planets orbiting it; determiners and adjectives are moons orbiting the nouns. The relations stay the same however the words are ordered.

sections.title: Heads, dependents and labels
sections.plain: Each arrow goes from a head word to a word that depends on it, labelled with the relation.
sections.body:
Each arc has a head (governor), a dependent (modifier) and a label (grammatical relation). Arrows are drawn from head to dependent; the main verb depends on an artificial ROOT.

"I saw a girl with a telescope": saw → I (nsubj), saw → girl (dobj), girl → a (det), with → telescope (pobj), telescope → a (det), and either saw → with (prep: I used the telescope) or girl → with (she had it). The whole ambiguity is a single arc, much simpler than two different bracketings.

Heads are usually content words (verbs head clauses, nouns head noun phrases). Dependency trees can be derived from constituency trees using head rules (the head child of each phrase).

sections.title: Well-formed trees and projectivity
sections.plain: Every word has exactly one head, there are no loops, everything connects to ROOT, and usually arcs don't cross.
sections.body:
A dependency structure is a directed graph G = (V, A). A valid tree is:

  1. Connected: every word is reachable from ROOT.
  2. Acyclic: if i → j then j does not reach i ($i\to j \Rightarrow j \not\to^* i$).
  3. Single-headed: every word except ROOT has exactly one incoming arc.
  4. Projective (usually): drawn above the sentence, no arcs cross; equivalently, each head and its descendants form a contiguous span.

Non-projective trees are linguistically real (e.g. "A hearing is scheduled on the issue today", where "on the issue" modifies "hearing" across "is scheduled"), and frequent in free-word-order languages. Transition parsers in their basic form only produce projective trees; graph-based MST parsing handles non-projective trees naturally.

sections.title: Universal Dependencies relations
sections.plain: A shared set of tags and relations so parsers and treebanks are comparable across languages.
sections.body:
The Universal Dependencies (UD) project provides consistent annotation across 100+ languages: universal POS tags (M6) and a standard inventory of relations, for example:

relationmeaningexample
nsubjnominal subjectHe sent
obj (dobj)direct objectsent a letter
iobjindirect objectsent her
amodadjectival modifiereconomic news
detdeterminerthe car
obl:tmodtemporal modifierleft yesterday
casecase marker / adpositionwith a telescope

UD favours content words as heads (prepositions attach to their noun as case), which makes structures more parallel across languages. Older English schemes (used in the examples here) use prep/pobj instead.

sections.title: Four families of dependency parsers
sections.plain: Dynamic programming, constraint satisfaction, greedy transitions, or global graph search.
sections.body:
1. Dynamic programming: CKY-style algorithms over spans; Eisner's algorithm parses projective dependencies in O(n³).
  2. Constraint satisfaction: start from all possible arcs and eliminate those violating hard grammatical constraints until a consistent structure remains.
  3. Deterministic transition-based parsing: a greedy left-to-right shift–reduce process whose next move is chosen by a trained classifier (e.g. MaltParser). Linear time.
  4. Graph-based parsing: score every possible arc and find the maximum spanning tree (e.g. MSTParser). Global optimisation.

The two most widely used, transition-based and graph-based, represent a classic trade-off: fast local decisions vs exact global search.

sections.title: Arc-eager transition parsing
sections.plain: Move words from a buffer onto a stack and add arcs between the stack top and the buffer front, one action at a time.
sections.body:
A configuration c = (S, B, A): stack S (starts as [ROOT]), buffer B (the words), arcs A (empty). The arc-eager actions:

  • SH (shift): push the buffer front onto the stack.
  • LA (left-arc): buffer front → stack top; pop the stack.
  • RA (right-arc): stack top → buffer front; push the buffer front.
  • RE (reduce): pop the stack top (it has its head and all dependents).

Trace: "He sent her a letter ."

actionstackbufferarc
SHROOT Hesent her a letter .
LAROOTsent her a letter .sent →SBJ He
RAROOT senther a letter .ROOT → sent
RAROOT sent hera letter .sent →IOBJ her
REROOT senta letter .
SHROOT sent aletter .
LAROOT sentletter .letter →DET a
RAROOT sent letter.sent →DOBJ letter
REROOT sent.
RAROOT sent .∅sent →PUNC .

Each word is shifted and reduced at most once, so the number of actions is linear in sentence length. (Shifting "a" before reducing "her" is an equally valid order.)

sections.title: Training the oracle and its cost
sections.plain: A classifier learns which action to take from features of the configuration; greedy choices are fast but errors cascade.
sections.body:
The "oracle" is a classifier choosing the next action. Training data comes from a treebank: each gold tree is converted into the sequence of configurations and correct actions. Features describe the configuration: POS and word of the stack top and buffer front, their existing dependents, distance, etc. The score of action t is $w\cdot f(c, t)$ and the parser picks $t^* = \arg\max_t w\cdot f(c,t)$.

Perceptron update when the prediction $t^*$ differs from the oracle action $t_o$: $w \leftarrow w + f(c, t_o) - f(c, t^*)$. Worked: features [stack empty, stack=Noun/buffer=Verb, stack=Verb/buffer=Noun], active feature 2. Weights SH [5, 5, 5], LA [5.5, 5.5, 5.5] (a left-arc bias). Prediction LA (5.5 > 5.0) is wrong; after one update SH = [5, 6, 5] (score 6.0) and LA = [5.5, 4.5, 5.5] (4.5): the decision is fixed.

Cost: parsing is O(n) and very fast, but decisions are greedy and never revisited, so an early mistake propagates (error cascading). Remedies: beam search, dynamic oracles, and neural classifiers (Chen & Manning 2014) over rich representations.

sections.title: Graph-based parsing and Chu-Liu-Edmonds
sections.plain: Score every possible arc and find the highest-scoring tree with a maximum spanning tree algorithm.
sections.body:
Build a complete directed graph over ROOT and the words; a model gives each arc i → j a score $w_{ij}$ (from features such as POS pair, direction, distance). The parse is the maximum spanning tree:

$$G' = \arg\max_{G\in T(G_x)} \sum_{(i,j)\in G} w_{ij}$$

Chu-Liu-Edmonds (directed MST, O(n²) with good implementations): (1) each word takes its highest-scoring incoming arc; if that is a tree, done. (2) Otherwise contract a cycle into one node. (3) Rescore: an arc entering the cycle at v gets its score − the score of v's internal arc + the cycle's total; arcs leaving take the best member's score. (4) Recurse, then unpack, breaking the internal arc displaced by the chosen entering arc.

Worked: "John saw Mary", scores root→John 9, root→saw 10, root→Mary 9, saw→John 30, saw→Mary 30, John→saw 20, Mary→John 11, John→Mary 3, Mary→saw 0. Greedy: John ← saw, saw ← John, Mary ← saw: cycle John↔saw (score 50). Into the cycle: root via saw 10 − 20 + 50 = 40, root via John 9 − 30 + 50 = 29, Mary via John 11 − 30 + 50 = 31. Choose root→saw; break John→saw. Result root→saw, saw→John, saw→Mary, total 70 (brute force agrees).

Learning is global: $w \leftarrow w + f(G_{\text{true}}) - f(G')$ over whole trees. Graph-based parsers handle non-projectivity and avoid greedy cascades; transition-based parsers are faster. Modern neural versions (biaffine scorers on BERT-like encoders) use the same decoding ideas.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Evaluation: unlabelled attachment score (UAS, % words with correct head) and labelled attachment score (LAS, head and label correct).
  • Arc-standard vs arc-eager: arc-standard adds right arcs only after the dependent has collected all its dependents; both are linear-time.
  • Swap transition lets transition parsers produce non-projective trees.
  • Uses: relation extraction often reads paths between entities in the dependency tree (e.g. nsubj–verb–obj triples feeding knowledge graphs, M12).

code.title: Arc-eager parsing with a static oracle
code.explain: Runs the arc-eager system on 'He sent her a letter .' with ROOT, choosing each action from the gold tree (a static oracle), printing every configuration and recovering all six arcs; then performs the worked perceptron update that fixes an LA-vs-SH mistake.
mistakes: Reducing a word before it has its head.
code.notes: A trained parser replaces the oracle with a classifier over features.

code.title: Chu-Liu-Edmonds maximum spanning tree
code.explain: Implements greedy selection, cycle detection, contraction with rescored arcs (root→C = 40, Mary→C = 31, C→Mary = 30) and unpacking for 'John saw Mary', returning root→saw, saw→John, saw→Mary (score 70), and checks it against brute force over all trees.
mistakes: Rescoring entering arcs without subtracting the broken internal arc.
